subs.title: Big-O for loops, nested loops, halving and extra storage

c.v: Both loops below look like a loop inside a loop. Count their steps:

The first makes n(n−1)/2 = 523,776 steps for n = 1024, which is O(n²). The second makes 1 + 2 + 4 + … + 512 = 1023 steps, which is O(n): its outer loop runs only log₂ n times, and the inner counts add up to less than 2n. You get Big-O by counting what the code does, not by looking at how its loops are nested.

Big-O describes how the number of steps grows as the input grows, ignoring constant factors: O(n) means at most a constant times n once n is large enough. To get it from code, add the costs of code that runs one after the other and keep the largest term, multiply the costs of nested loops, and count a loop whose variable halves or doubles as log n. When the input has two sizes, keep both. O(n + m) and O(n·m) are different answers, and collapsing them into n loses what an interviewer is asking for.
Space works the same way.
Extra space

is the memory you use beyond the input: new containers, the output if you build it, and the recursion stack, where every level of depth counts. In an interview, give both time and extra space and name the variables, for example "O(n log n) time and O(n) extra space, where n is the number of intervals".

c.v: For the measurement, here is one way to do it. The timings vary from run to run, so there is no fixed output to compare against. Look at the ratios between rows.
This program pushes 20 elements into an empty vector and prints a line each time the capacity changes.
Counted
counts how many times the vector moves an element into a new block of memory.

blocks.text:
size  1 -> capacity 1
size  2 -> capacity 2
size  3 -> capacity 4
size  5 -> capacity 8
size  9 -> capacity 16
size 17 -> capacity 32
20 pushes moved 31 elements in total

c.v: Six of the 20 pushes found the vector full. Each of them allocated a block twice as large, moved every element across and freed the old block. They moved 0, 1, 2, 4, 8 and 16 elements. The other 14 pushes moved nothing.

So a single push can cost O(n), but a sequence of pushes can't average out that badly. Because the capacity doubles, the moves needed to reach n elements add up to less than 2n, and the cost per push over the whole sequence is constant. That is what
amortised O(1)
means. The growth factor is the library's choice. GCC's libstdc++ doubles the capacity. Microsoft's library grows it by 1.5, which is still amortised O(1), with more reallocations.
Amortised cost is often confused with average cost. An amortised bound holds for every sequence of operations, whatever the input. An average is taken over inputs.
std::unordered_map::find
is O(1) on average, but when every key lands in the same bucket it is O(n), and no argument about sequences changes that.
If you know the final size,
reserve(n)

allocates once and the moves disappear. Growth also has a cost that matters more than time: it invalidates every pointer, reference and iterator into the vector. The topic on iterators and invalidation covers the bugs this causes.

c.v: Solution
With
reserve(20)
, the program prints no capacity lines and the move count is 0. The capacity is already 20 when
last
is read, and it never changes inside the loop.
A doubling vector reallocates about 20 times on the way to a million elements, because 2²⁰ is about 10⁶.
Without
noexcept
, the vector copies instead of moving. When it grows,
std::vector

promises that a push which throws leaves the vector as it was: the strong exception guarantee. If a move threw halfway through, some elements would already have left the old block and that promise would be broken. So the vector moves elements only when the move constructor can't throw, which it checks with
std::move_if_noexcept
, and copies them otherwise. That is the practical reason to mark move constructors
noexcept
